prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B005 alone, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After the full exchange I can also answer the chair's first question in one sentence. The 2005 prize gave us a ruler that counts optical cycles and the 2012 prize gave us control of one trapped quantum system, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate idea: choosing the trapping wavelength so that both clock levels shift equally removes the light shift, and the Lamb-Dicke regime removes motional shifts, for thousands of neutral atoms at once. That is more than averaging. Without the magic condition the many-atom trap could not be used at all, and it is why the systematic uncertainty fell to about 1e-18 and the stability gain over single-ion clocks is so large. As an instrument builder I weigh what has been checked, and this has been checked: JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL reproduce the performance and compare clocks over fibre links. It already gives redshift measurements over millimetres, tighter bounds on varying constants and ultralight dark matter couplings. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: all eight members independently name the same two people, with Katori holding the proposal and first strontium realization and Ye the record accuracy and many-body control.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is not zero, and a sceptic can still call the lattice clock an extremely good step along an honoured road. I answer this on mechanism, but the committee should not pretend the question is closed, and the citation must be drafted narrowly so that it does not repeat the comb or reward metrology in general. A second weakness is that a measured variation of a constant or a violation has not been found, so the physics payoff so far is tightened bounds and a new measurement capability, not a new phenomenon. Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and Derevianko lie outside two names, and I cannot verify the priority chronology myself. Atomic physics is outside my expertise, so I rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Danielsson, and I support asking outside experts to check Katori's 2001-2003 proposal against the first strontium lattice-clock measurements before the vote is final.

responses.point: Eriksson asked whether the many-atom lattice is a real conceptual advance over single-ion clocks or mainly a gain in averaging, and he accepts that the Wineland comparison is the harder one.
responses.response: I take this as the key question and my answer is that it is both, but the conceptual part comes first. Averaging over many atoms is only useful if the atoms are interrogated without motional and Stark shifts, and the magic-wavelength condition with Lamb-Dicke confinement is what delivers that. Without the idea there is no gain to average. The ion clock reached its accuracy through a different route, a single well-isolated particle, and it pays for that in signal. I would put this into the committee's working text as the distinction from 2012. I also thank him for moving to B005 from B043 and for keeping B014 as the alternative if B005 stalls, which fits my own list.

responses.point: Johansson moved B005 to first, asks for a narrow citation around the lattice-clock invention and its 1e-18 realization, and in round 1 raised waiting for the SI second redefinition as a marker of impact.
responses.response: I agree on the narrow citation and I would draft the wording on the lattice clock and not on timekeeping or optical metrology as a field. On waiting, I still say no. The redefinition is a timetable set by metrology bodies; the physics is already demonstrated and independently reproduced. What would change my answer is not the redefinition but a discrepancy between laboratories at the 1e-18 level, which would suggest the systematics are not understood. I see no sign of that. I also note his question to me about IceCube, which I take up in my response to Lindroth.

responses.point: Lindroth stresses the quantitative agreement between calculated magic wavelengths and blackbody and lattice shifts and measurement, treats the priority chronology as a drafting matter, and asks whether the diffuse neutrino flux alone could carry an IceCube citation.
responses.response: Her point on theory and measurement meeting at this precision is exactly the kind of check I want, and it is why I am comfortable with the maturity. On the diffuse flux, my honest view is that the observation of a high-energy astrophysical flux is the solid part of IceCube and the source identifications are not yet at the same level, so a citation resting on the flux would be defensible in science but would still need the credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering sorted out with outside experts. That is why I keep B035 as an alternative for a later year and not as a second part now. I agree that the chronology is for the wording, but I would still ask the experts to read the primary papers.

responses.point: Olsson wants Katori's 2001-2003 proposal checked against the first strontium lattice-clock measurements, and would keep IceCube for a later year because source evidence is at the few-sigma level and attribution is shaky.
responses.response: I agree with the verification step and propose it as the one concrete request to outside experts: the proposal, the first lattice-clock measurements, and Ye's record accuracy results. I largely accept her position on IceCube; after the exchange I no longer see a case for adding B035 as a second part, since a two-part prize with only a subset of Halzen, Karle and Spiering would be unfair to the omitted names, which answers the chair's last question for me. Where I still differ is the timing: the discovery is over a decade old and I would not wait indefinitely.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B005 as the most defensible choice and asks whether waiting for the SI second adds maturity or only delay, and whether the committee regards precision measurement as a discovery in the Nobel sense.
responses.response: I think waiting adds delay and not maturity, for the reason given above. On discovery versus invention, the statutes say discovery or invention, and the lattice clock is an invention that gave a measurement nobody could make before. I also take his own point that B014 is unsettled because the pairing mechanism and sample variability are still moving. I keep B014 in my alternatives but I would not put it ahead of B005 on maturity.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the mechanism argument that separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.

Priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and parallel lattice-clock ideas, and whether Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde or Derevianko have a claim that two names cannot reflect; I cannot check this myself.
Whether outside experts confirm that Katori and Ye are the decisive pair and that the 1e-18 accuracy figures stand against the primary papers.
Whether IceCube (B035) would be fairly credited to any three names, and whether the source identifications will firm up, which matters only for later years.
statement.conflict_note: My profile lists membership in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and a field (astroparticle physics, space and balloon instruments) adjacent to IceCube (B035), which was my opening first choice and remains an alternative. I am not an IceCube member and the profile shows no direct tie to Halzen, Karle or Spiering. I have no apparent conflict regarding B005 (Katori, Ye) or the other shortlisted candidates. As chair I note that my change of position was driven by the first-round discussion and not by any external contact.
